cards.front: Picture size = real size × {{c1::magnification}}.
cards.back: Picture size is how big a thing looks through the microscope.
cards.quote: A microscope makes things look bigger: picture size = real size × magnification, where picture size is how big a thing looks.

cards.front: What is the eye line?
cards.back: The smallest size most people can make out by eye at reading distance: about 100 µm, or 0.1 mm.
cards.quote: At a normal reading distance, most people can make out something only when it is bigger than about 100 micrometres (µm), or 0.1 mm.

cards.front: A cell's picture is bigger than the eye line. Why might you still not see its shape?
cards.back: Size is not enough. The lens must also show the detail clearly, and the cell must stand out from its background.
cards.why: A stain helps a cell stand out.
cards.quote: To see a cell's shape, the lens must also show the detail clearly, and the cell must stand out from its background (a stain helps).

cards.front: A school microscope has a 10x eyepiece. You use the 40x objective. What is the total magnification?
cards.back: Multiply the two lenses: 10 × 40 = 400x.
cards.quote: Multiply the two to get the total magnification: 10 × 4 = 40x, 10 × 10 = 100x and 10 × 40 = 400x.
cards.section: How small is too small to see?

cards.front: The circle of the slide you see through a microscope is the {{c1::field of view}}.
cards.back: At higher power, this circle shows a smaller part of the slide.
cards.quote: At higher power you see a smaller circle of the slide. This circle is the field of view.
cards.section: How small is too small to see?

cards.front: A bacterium is about 2 µm long. Does its picture pass the eye line (about 100 µm) at 40x? At 100x?
cards.back: At 40x: 2 × 40 = 80 µm, so no. At 100x: 2 × 100 = 200 µm, so it passes the size test.
cards.why: Passing the size test is not enough: an unstained bacterium is still hard to make out at 100x.
cards.quote: At 40x: 2 × 40 = 80 µm, under the eye line, so no.
cards.section: How small is too small to see?

cards.front: A Paramecium is about 200 µm long, twice the eye line. Yet a drop of pond water with Paramecium in it looks clear. Why?
cards.back: A Paramecium is nearly colourless, so it is a faint speck that is easy to miss. It does not stand out from its background.
cards.why: Most other living things in the drop are under 100 µm, too small for the eye at all.
cards.quote: But a Paramecium is nearly colourless, a faint speck that is easy to miss
cards.section: How small is too small to see?

cards.front: A living thing made of just one cell, such as a Paramecium, is {{c1::unicellular}}.
cards.quote: Some organisms, such as a Paramecium, are just one cell: they are unicellular.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: Living things made of many cells, such as you and an oak tree, are {{c1::multicellular}}.
cards.quote: Others, such as you and an oak tree, are multicellular, made of many cells.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: What are the three parts of the cell theory?
cards.back: 1. All living things are made of one or more cells. 2. The cell is the basic unit of life. 3. All cells come from cells that already exist.
cards.quote: All living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. All cells come from cells that already exist.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: Why is the cell called the basic unit of life?
cards.back: It is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life.
cards.quote: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: A tiny animal in pond water is too small to see well without a microscope. Must it be made of only one cell?
cards.back: No. Tiny does not always mean one cell. Some pond animals this small are made of many cells.
cards.why: The cell theory only says every living thing is made of one or more cells.
cards.quote: Tiny does not always mean one cell: some animals in pond water are too small to see well, but they are made of many cells.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: Are all cells alike? Give an example.
cards.back: No. A red blood cell is a small disc, while a nerve cell can have long, thin branches.
cards.quote: Cells are not all alike: a red blood cell is a small disc, and a nerve cell can have long, thin branches.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells

cards.front: How is a theory in science different from a theory in everyday talk?
cards.back: In everyday talk, a theory can mean a hunch. In science, it is a well-tested explanation backed by a great deal of evidence.
cards.quote: In everyday talk, a theory can mean a hunch. In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation backed by a great deal of evidence.

cards.front: Can a well-tested scientific theory, such as the cell theory, ever change?
cards.back: Yes. It can change if strong new evidence appears. The cell theory changed when better tools gave new evidence.
cards.quote: A theory can still change if strong new evidence appears

cards.front: You keep magnifying a cell with a light microscope, far past 400x. Will you keep seeing new, smaller parts?
cards.back: Not forever. Light blurs details closer than about 0.2 µm, so more magnification gives a bigger blur, not new detail.
cards.why: This limit holds for the best standard light microscopes with ordinary glass lenses.
cards.quote: Past that point, more magnification only makes a bigger blur, not new detail.

cards.front: What does an electron microscope use instead of light?
cards.back: A beam of electrons. It shows smaller parts inside cells than a light microscope can.
cards.quote: For those, scientists built the electron microscope, which uses a beam of electrons instead of light

cards.front: A human red blood cell is 7.7 µm wide. The light microscope limit is about 0.2 µm. How many times wider is the red blood cell than that limit?
cards.back: 7.7 ÷ 0.2 = 38.5 times wider.
cards.quote: How many times wider is a red blood cell than the 0.2 µm light-microscope limit? Divide 7.7 by 0.2.

cards.front: A frog egg is about 1,000 µm across. How many millimetres is that?
cards.back: 100 µm = 0.1 mm, so about 1,000 µm is about 1 mm.
cards.quote: A frog egg is about 1,000 µm across. How many millimetres is that?

cards.front: You compare slides of onion skin and pond water with slides of sand and salt. Why also look at a clean slide with only the distilled water used on the others?
cards.back: It is a blank control. It shows what comes from the slide or the water, so you do not mistake it for cells.
cards.quote: Blank control: a clean slide with only the distilled water used on the other slides, so you can tell what comes from the slide or water.

cards.front: Cork is not alive, yet under a microscope it shows boxes like cells. Does this break the idea that only living things show cells?
cards.back: No. The boxes are walls left by plant cells. Cork is not alive now, but it was once alive.
cards.why: Not alive now is not the same as never alive.
cards.quote: Both are walls left by plant cells. Not alive now is not the same as never alive.

cards.front: Use cell sizes to explain why the cell theory came only after microscopes were invented.
cards.back: Most cells are about 1 to 100 µm across, at or below the eye line, so most people could not make them out by eye. Microscopes made cells visible and gave the evidence for the theory.
cards.why: Picture size = real size × magnification lets a tiny cell pass the eye line.
cards.quote: Learning this took about two hundred years and better tools, starting with cork boxes like the ones you just zoomed into.
cards.section: What the microscope showed: living things are made of cells
